dct_description_sm: Investigations of the ecology of foxes in the Prudhoe Bay area began in the mid-1970s, when predictions were made that increased availability of human food could result in higher  productivity, increased density, and dampened population fluctuations of arctic foxes (Alopex lagopus), the primary species of fox in the region. The red fox (Vulpes vulpes) also occurs on the North Slope, and population numbers have been increasing greatly in the last few years. Increased densities of foxes could also affect the populations of prey species, particularly tundra nesting birds. Since the early 1990s, arctic foxes have caused catastrophic nesting failure of the Howe Island Snow Goose colony in some years. In addition, foxes are carriers of rabies and may pose a health risk to oil field workers, as well as other residents. Red foxes seem to be increasingly common in areas of the oil fields previously occupied by arctic foxes.
dct_title_s: Fox Den Monitoring in Greater Prudhoe Bay, Alaska
